question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question asks specifically about a best-of-five-games-to-11 match and the third game. The standard Laws source [laws-8.1.3] gives the general third-game change-of-ends rule, while [alt-best-of-5-games-11:8.1.3] gives the Alternative Laws rule for the best-of-5-games-11 format and directly answers the third-game timing, including its condition. Together they answer the question; no additional search is needed.
answer.answer: Standard rule first: under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)". question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly covered by the given sources. ITTO 5.9.1.4 says a player calling ‘fault’ to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. Law 13.4.5 makes it a fault if, in play, a player deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting. Law 7.3 gives the consequence: the side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, and the side winning a rally adds a point. The partner-shouting clause 5.9.1.3 is a contrast only and does not apply because the shout was to the opponent during play.
answer.answer: The opponent’s shout of ‘fault!’ while you were playing your shot is treated as a deliberate distraction: under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, a player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke “shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)”. Under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 13.4.5 makes it a fault “if, in play, a player: deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures”. Ruling: fault against the opponent; under Law 7.3, your side wins the rally because the opposing side committed a fault, and the side winning a rally adds a point to its score.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: when a rally is replayed, and every situation that is a let. The Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, clauses 14.1–14.3 answer both: 14.1 says who calls a let, 14.2 lists the let situations, and 14.3 says what happens when a let occurs. Clause 14.2.3 ended with a colon, so read_clause was used to obtain its subclauses 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2. A further search confirmed 14.2.7 is the catch-all and found only Para Badminton exceptions (14.2.3.1.1 / 14.2.3.2.1), which are not mentioned because the question is not about para play. ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.2 adds the adjacent-court shuttle clarification. Together these sources fully answer the question.
answer.answer: Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), a rally is replayed when a ‘let’ occurs: play since the last service does not count and the player who served last serves again (Law 14.3). A ‘let’ is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Law 14.1). Law 14.2 states that it shall be a ‘let’ in every one of the following situations: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) (14.2.1); (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted (14.2.2); (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top (14.2.3.1), or after passing over the net is caught in the net (14.2.3.2) — both under 14.2.3, ‘after the service is returned, the shuttle is:’; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle (14.2.4); (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach (14.2.5); (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision (14.2.6); or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred (14.2.7). Separately, the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26) clarify that a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court is not automatically a let: no let is called there if, in the umpire’s opinion, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players (ITTO 5.9.1.2).

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding cut, and (2) who may come on court to help. The sources cover both. itto-5.14.2 directly addresses a blood-flowing injury and states when the delay ends; itto-3.6.1.4 gives the Referee's time expectation and the warning about exploiting the injury; itto-5.14.1 covers who examines the player, the ban on treatment causing undue delay on court, and that the Umpire times the delay; itto-3.6.1.3 gives the maximum number of persons allowed on court to assist and the fairness requirement for the opposing side. Together these answer the question fully, so no further searching is needed.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: For a blood-flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise [itto-5.14.2]. The Referee must resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so play can be resumed or abandoned, and may point to potential disqualification if the player is suspected of exploiting the injury to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play [itto-3.6.1.4]. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court, and the Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury [itto-5.14.1]. Who can come on court: The Umpire must try to determine the severity as quickly as possible and call the Referee onto court if necessary; the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court, and the Tournament Doctor examines the player and advises about the severity [itto-5.14.1]. The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness shall allow the opposing side the same consideration [itto-3.6.1.3]. All of these come from Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.

The Referee may need to point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind, or if the player repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play.

The Umpire must try to determine the severity of the problem as quickly as possible and call the Referee onto court, if necessary. The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6). The Tournament Doctor shall examine the player and advise the player about the severity of injury or sickness. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court. question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and its score when water makes the court unplayable mid-game. The given sources plus two searched clauses cover this fully: ITTO 5.11.2 allows suspension for circumstances affecting playing conditions; ITTO 5.11.3 (given) covers a court that is temporarily not playable — Umpire calls the Referee and play is suspended until the court is suitable again; ITTO 5.11.4 (found) gives the call 'Play is suspended' and noting 'S'; Laws 16.3.3 (found) states the existing score stands and play resumes from that point; ITTO 5.11.5 (given) gives the resumption procedure. Nothing is missing.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court makes it temporarily not playable, so play is suspended. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.2, play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire 'if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions', and under Clause 5.11.3, 'If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.' When play is suspended, the Umpire calls 'Play is suspended' and notes 'S' on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.4). The score is not affected: under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.3, 'If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.' When play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls 'Are you ready?' followed by the score and 'Play' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.5).

citations.quote: Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions.

If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly covered by itto-5.9.1.6, which addresses a player throwing sweat/contaminating the court and says the umpire shall remind the player, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. To say what Law 16.7 allows, laws-16.7.1 and its subclauses list warning, fault after warning, and fault for flagrant breach; laws-16.7.2 adds that on faulting the umpire reports immediately to the Referee, who may disqualify. answer.answer: Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.6, a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings 'shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary.' If Law 16.7 is applied, under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 16.7.1 the umpire administers the breach by 'issuing a warning to the offending side; or' 'faulting the offending side, if previously warned; or' 'faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach.' Under Clause 16.7.2, 'On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match.'

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question assumes the line judge was “unsighted.” The sources cover that: ITTO 7.0 (5) tells the line judge to signal unsighted, and says that when a line judge is unsighted the Umpire makes the immediate call; ITTO 2.5 and Laws 14.2.6 cover the case where no decision can be made (let, or IRS if in use), and ITTO 5.8.9 covers IRS “NO DECISION.” Together they answer what happens to the rally, with conditions.
answer.answer: The rally is not automatically a let. The line judge must signal “unsighted” immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5). Because a line judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately make the line call: “Out” if the shuttle landed outside the line, or the score/“Service over” if it landed “in” (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.8.3 and 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.2). More generally, when another official is unsighted the Umpire shall make the decision; only when no decision can be made is a “let” called, unless IRS is in use, in which case IRS is used to decide the line call (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 2.5). Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it is a “let” if “a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision” (Law 14.2.6). If IRS indicates “NO DECISION,” it is a “Let” when the original call is “Unsighted” (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.8.9).

“Out” when the shuttle lands outside the line and then call either the score or “Service over” and then the score; or
The score or “Service over” and then the score when the shuttle lands “in”; or

When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision. When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call (BWF Statutes, Section 4.1.8, Regulation 1.2).
a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or
If the Instant Review System indicates “NO DECISION”, it shall be a “Let” if the original call is “Unsighted”, otherwise the original challenged decision shall stand.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand court-side during a match. The directly on-point source is itto-5.12.2, which states coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during permitted intervals, cross-referencing Law 16.2. Laws-16.2.1 and laws-16.2.2 define those permitted intervals (60 seconds when the leading score reaches 11; 120 seconds between games). itto-5.12.3 and itto-5.12.5 concern moving chairs and communicating, not standing, so they only add context. Together the sources fully answer the question: standing court-side is prohibited except during the permitted intervals.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2, coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match, except during the permitted intervals under Law 16.2. Those permitted intervals, under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (except Handicap matches) (Law 16.2.1), and not exceeding 120 seconds between games (Law 16.2.2). So your coach may stand court-side only during those intervals, not during play. Separately, if the coach wishes to move to another court, he must do so while the shuttle is not in play (itto-5.12.2), and he may not move his chair from its designated position without the Referee's permission (itto-5.12.3).

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Weight of a plastic (non-feathered) shuttle: laws-2.3.3 says a non-feathered shuttle's measurements and weight are as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6, with up to 10 per cent variation acceptable; laws-2.2.6 gives the feathered shuttle weight of 4.74 to 5.50 grams, which 2.3.3 incorporates by reference. (2) A special shuttle for hot/stuffy conditions: laws-2.4 allows modifications to the specifications with the approval of the Member Association concerned where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable, provided there is no variation in general design, speed and flight. Both parts are answered by the given sources, so no further search is needed.
answer.answer: Plastic (non-feathered) shuttle weight: the weight must be as in Law 2.2.6 — 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because of the difference in specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials compared with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clauses 2.3.3 and 2.2.6). So a plastic shuttle may weigh roughly 4.27 to 6.05 grams (10 per cent either side of 4.74–5.50 g). For your hot, stuffy hall: yes, a modified shuttle may be used, but only subject to two conditions — there must be 'no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle', and the modification must be made 'with the approval of the Member Association concerned', and only 'in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable' (Clause 2.4). A hot hall alone does not automatically permit it; you need the Member Association's approval and the shuttle must fly like the standard one.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card for misconduct during warm-up, before 'Play', costs a point now; and (2) whether the card goes on the player's record after the tournament. itto-5.17.10 directly covers pre-'Play' misconduct on the Field of Play: cards given have no effect on the score but are taken into account if further offences occur during the match, cross-referencing Law 16.7.1.2 (faulting the offending side if previously warned). itto-5.17.3 confirms a yellow card is the warning. For the post-tournament part, itto-3.7.3 (After the Tournament) requires the Referee to send BWF (or CC) a report on yellow and red cards that may trigger further sanctions, with itto-3.7.3.1 allowing the Referee to decide not to report a card in a specific observed case, and itto-5.17.2 requiring the Umpire to record and report the incident to the Referee. Together these answer both parts, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer:
No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" is called is treated as a warning (yellow card), and any card given before "Play" "shall have no effect on the score of the match" — but it "shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match", meaning that under Law 16.7.1.2 the umpire faults the offending side "if previously warned". (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.10; Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 16.7.1.2.)

As for after the tournament: the card does not stay only on the court — the Umpire must "record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.2), and "immediately after the tournament" the Referee "shall ... send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3). The one exception: the Referee may decide not to report a card if the Referee or a Deputy observed the situation and decides the card should not have been issued (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3.1). So the yellow card is reported after the tournament and may trigger further sanctions, but it has no effect on the score of the match in which it was given.
